sentences.text: Barawertornis is an extinct genus of bird that contains only one species, Barawertornis tedfordi. This animal belongs to the extinct family Dromornithidae.
The skeleton displays clear anatomical features suited for a running lifestyle.
Most femurs show a caudal intermuscular line, although this feature is missing in specimen QM F30352.
The outer part of the thigh bone is roughly one-third as wide as the inner part.
The main shaft of the lower leg bone curves slightly from side to side.
A hole for blood vessels exists at the end of the leg bone in Barawertornis, but this is usually absent in most Dromornis stirtoni specimens.
The skull bone above the jaw joint has a dorsal process, a trait also found in Dromornis planei.
The lower jaw lacks a specific opening at the back.
The process at the base of the skull is deep and very strong.
Barawertornis tedfordi is the smallest known dromornithid species, weighing between 26.9 and 79 kg.
Fossil evidence reveals unhealed bite marks and fractures on the bones of this bird.
Fragmentary remains of a dromornithid were first reported from the Carl Creek Limestone in Queensland in 1968 by Richard H. Tedford.
Patricia Vickers-Rich established the genus and species Barawertornis tedfordi in 1979 based on remains found by Richard H. Tedford.
Skull material was referred to Barawertornis in a 2016 study by Trevor Worthy and colleagues.
Barawertornis was first described in 1979 by Patricia Vickers-Rich.
Barawertornis was likely a browser that ate leaves and fruit, similar to other dromornithids.
A 2024 study suggests that Barawertornis, like other dromornithids, may have had adaptations for an aquatic feeding style.
Researchers hypothesize that unhealed bite marks and fractures on a Barawertornis femur were caused by a crocodilian predator like Baru.
Gouges on a damaged Barawertornis tarsometatarsus are attributed to predators, scavengers, or trampling, though the exact cause is unknown.
Barawertornis was originally assigned to the family Dromornithidae and placed in the subfamily Barawertornithinae.
The genus name Barawertornis combines an Aboriginal word for 'ground' and the Ancient Greek word for 'bird'.
The species name tedfordi honors Richard H. Tedford for his discoveries of tertiary avian fauna in Australia.
Barawertornis lived during the Oligocene and Miocene epochs in Queensland and South Australia.
Barawertornis fossils are found in Late Oligocene and Early Miocene limestone deposits at the Riversleigh World Heritage Area in Queensland.
During the Late Oligocene, the Riversleigh habitat consisted of open forests with sclerophyllous vegetation and deciduous vine thickets.
Barawertornis fossils have been reported from the Leaf Locality of the Wipajiri Formation in northern South Australia.
The age of the Wipajiri Formation site is uncertain, with studies suggesting it dates to either the Early or Middle Miocene.
Barawertornis lived between 23.04 and 15.98 million years ago (Aquitanian to Burdigalian stages).
It is debated whether Barawertornis belongs to the Ilbandornis lineage, with some researchers suggesting similarities in the crania support this.
